meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'England is a nation of shopkeepers'?
meta.ogDescription: Napoleon gets the credit, but the phrase is Adam Smith’s (1776), turned into an insult by Bertrand Barère in 1794. The Napoleon link is doubtful.

answer.label: Not Napoleon Bonaparte — the phrase is Adam Smith’s
answer.sourceLine: The phrase “a nation of shopkeepers” is Adam Smith’s, from The Wealth of Nations (1776) ↗, and was turned into an anti-British jibe by the revolutionary Bertrand Barère in 1794. There is no contemporaneous evidence that Napoleon ever said “England is a nation of shopkeepers” — the attribution rests only on a doubted later memoir.

source.heading: Where the phrase actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations (1776)

source.excerpt: To found a great empire for the sole purpose of raising up a people of customers, may at first sight appear a project fit only for a nation of shopkeepers.
trail: The phrase appears in Adam Smith’s The Wealth of Nations (1776) ↗: “…a project fit only for a nation of shopkeepers.”
An even earlier related form comes from Josiah Tucker, Dean of Gloucester, in 1766: “what is true of a shopkeeper is true of a shopkeeping nation,” per Word Histories ↗.
The disparaging anti-British use was popularised by French revolutionary Bertrand Barère in a June 1794 National Convention speech, not by Napoleon, per Wikipedia ↗.
No contemporaneous French newspaper records Napoleon using the phrase; the attribution traces to Barry O’Meara’s memoir Napoleon in Exile (1822), whose reliability is questioned, per Wikipedia ↗.
source.excerptNote: Adam Smith’s original 1776 wording. Note that Smith uses “a nation of shopkeepers” as an abstract figure of speech — the punchy sentence “England is a nation of shopkeepers” put in Napoleon’s mouth is a later, sharpened paraphrase.

author.name: Adam Smith
author.heading: About Adam Smith
author.bio: Adam Smith was a Scottish philosopher and the founding thinker of modern economics, best known for The Wealth of Nations (1776). It is there that the phrase “a nation of shopkeepers” enters English — as a wry description of a commercial empire, not the sneering put-down later attributed to Napoleon.

copyAttribution: Phrase originates with Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations (1776); popularised as an anti-British insult by Bertrand Barère (1794). Commonly misattributed to Napoleon Bonaparte, who most likely never said it.

misattribution.heading: How Napoleon got the credit
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the most durable quotations pinned on Napoleon — but the phrase predates his fame and the evidence he ever used it is thin.

items.why: Popularly “England is a nation of shopkeepers” is credited to Napoleon as a sneer at Britain, but no contemporaneous French source records him saying it. The claim rests on Barry O’Meara’s memoir Napoleon in Exile (1822), whose reliability is doubted, per Wikipedia ↗.
The derogatory anti-British use was actually launched by the revolutionary Bertrand Barère in a National Convention speech in June 1794, years before Napoleon’s rise, per Word Histories ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The phrase is Adam Smith’s (1776) and was weaponised against Britain by Bertrand Barère in 1794 — Napoleon most likely never said it, per Wikipedia ↗.

context.heading: Why it stuck to Napoleon
lead: The insult fit the story England wanted to tell about itself. During the Napoleonic Wars the British press circulated the “nation of shopkeepers” jibe — sometimes crediting “the French,” sometimes Napoleon — and Britons cheerfully reclaimed it: a trading, seafaring people who out-lasted a continental tyrant. A memorable enemy makes a better story than an economist or a half-forgotten revolutionary, so the line migrated onto Napoleon and stayed there.
context.pull: The phrase is Adam Smith’s; the sneer is Barère’s; the fame is Napoleon’s.
